analysis.one_liner: Overhauls health insurance markets, creates state insurance marketplaces with subsidies, and adds a government-run plan.
analysis.headline: The Senate's health committee reported this health reform bill in September 2009 and placed it on the Senate calendar, where it sat; it never received a Senate vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have banned insurers from rejecting or charging more to people with pre-existing conditions, stopped lifetime benefit caps, let young adults stay on a parent's plan until 26, and required coverage of preventive care. It would have created state 'Gateways' — marketplaces where people and small businesses could shop for plans with income-based subsidies, including a government-run community health insurance option alongside private plans. It also required most people to carry insurance (with a tax surtax on those who don't), charged employers whose workers lack qualifying coverage, and included a long-term disability insurance program, menu calorie labeling, workforce grants, and a pathway for cheaper copies of biologic drugs after 12 years of exclusivity.
analysis.who_benefits: Uninsured and underinsured Americans, especially people with pre-existing conditions who could be refused coverage today, low-income households receiving premium credits, young adults up to age 26, small businesses eligible for tax credits, coal miners and survivors under the black lung provisions, and rural and underserved communities gaining community health center and workforce funding.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The uninsured and people with pre-existing conditions

how_it_helps.text: Bars health insurers from denying coverage or setting eligibility rules based on health status, medical history, claims experience, or genetic information, and prohibits pre-existing condition exclusions.
Limits premium rating to age (no more than 2-to-1), tobacco use, family size, and geography — insurers could no longer charge more by gender, occupation, or health.
Prohibits lifetime or annual dollar limits on benefits and requires coverage of dependents until age 26.

Creates American Health Benefit Gateways (marketplaces) in every state offering qualified health plans, pays premium credits to the Gateway for eligible individuals, gives low-income enrollees reduced cost-sharing tiers, and pays small employers a credit toward their employees' coverage.
Requires every Gateway to include a government-run community health insurance option offering essential health benefits nationwide.
Requires coverage of evidence-based preventive services and women's preventive health without significant cost-sharing, and establishes a Prevention and Public Health Fund.
Establishes the CLASS Act, a voluntary national disability insurance program funded by payroll deductions to pay for long-term services and supports that help people stay independent.
Creates the first regulatory pathway for biosimilars — lower-priced copies of expensive biologic drugs — and expands the 340B discount program to more hospitals and to inpatient drugs.
Reauthorizes community health centers, expands health professions training and loan repayment, and requires reasonable break time and a private space for nursing mothers at work.
Requires chain restaurants with 20 or more locations to post calories on menus and menu boards, and large vending machine operators to post calorie signs.

analysis.who_pays: Uninsured individuals would owe a surtax for not carrying coverage; employers not offering qualifying coverage (or contributing at least 60% of premiums) would owe payments per uncovered worker, though small employers are exempt; taxpayers fund the premium credits, public health fund, and workforce programs; brand-name biologic drug makers keep 12 years of market exclusivity before cheaper biosimilars can reach patients; health insurers face new market rules but gain millions of subsidized, mandate-driven customers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Uninsured individuals, larger employers, and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The individual surtax would penalize people who go without coverage, including many who remain uninsured because coverage is still unaffordable for them.

The bill locks in a 12-year period after a biologic drug's approval before any biosimilar can be approved — far longer than generic drugs wait — delaying price competition on some of the most expensive medicines in American health care.

The CLASS Act relies entirely on voluntary payroll-deduction premiums with no tax funding; the structure was widely criticized as fiscally unsustainable, and the program was later abandoned by HHS and repealed.
Existing plans are grandfathered from the new market rules, so many people enrolled on the date of enactment — and new employees joining those plans — would not benefit from the protections.

The employer payments apply only to employers not offering qualifying coverage, creating incentives to keep workers' hours or coverage just below the thresholds, and self-insured group plans are exempt from the premium-rating and guaranteed-issue rules.
Critics of the individual mandate argued, and the Supreme Court later held in another form, that forcing people to buy insurance or pay a penalty raised serious legal and fairness questions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On balance this draft leaned toward helping ordinary people: it regulated insurers rather than entrenching them, and it was the version of health reform that contained a government-run public option competing with private plans. Its main costs fall on taxpayers, on uninsured individuals facing the surtax, and on patients who would wait 12 years for cheaper biosimilar versions of brand biologics — a concession to the biotech industry that the generic drug industry also opposed. The CLASS Act was a design flaw the sponsors never fixed.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate health committee reported the bill and placed it on the Senate calendar in September 2009, but the full Senate never took it up; the majority leader instead combined it with the Finance Committee's draft into the merged bill that became the Affordable Care Act, and this bill died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on September 17, 2009 by Senator Harkin.

The same day, the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee reported it as an original measure, without a written report, and it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 161.
The bill had no cosponsors, which is normal for an original measure reported directly by a committee.
No further action was taken on the bill — no floor debate, no vote, no amendments — before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never got a Senate vote and was folded into the merged ACA, its strongest consumer provisions — the government-run community health insurance option — were dropped in the final law, and the 12-year biologic exclusivity survived. Private health insurers and brand-name biologic drug makers came out ahead of this bill's original design, though millions of Americans later gained coverage and market protections through the ACA that emerged from it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and brand drug makers, versus the original design

for.name: Tom Harkin
for.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and reported it to the full Senate from his committee as an original measure on September 17, 2009.

for.name: Senate HELP Committee majority
for.role: Majority members of the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
for.what_they_did: Produced and reported the committee's comprehensive health reform draft directly to the Senate calendar without a written report.

for.name: Barack Obama
for.what_they_did: Pushed congressional Democrats to complete comprehensive health reform legislation during 2009-2010, giving committee drafts like this one a path into the final merged bill.

against.name: Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor; instead merged this committee draft with the Finance Committee's draft into a single bill that the Senate debated in late 2009.

against.name: 40 of 40 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Opposed the comprehensive health reform effort; no Republican supported the final ACA, and the party fought it with procedural delays throughout 2009-2010.

against.name: Health insurance industry
against.role: AHIP and the health insurance industry
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against the government-run public option contained in this draft and against provisions restricting their rating and underwriting practices.

sides.party_line_note: The bill itself never reached a floor vote, but the health reform fight it was part of split cleanly by party: Democrats produced and passed the reform through a party-line process, while Senate Republicans opposed it unanimously.

industries.note: The bill routes all subsidized coverage through private qualified health plans sold on the state Gateways, and the individual surtax plus employer payments channel millions of new customers to insurers — locking them in as the delivery system. In exchange, insurers give up pre-existing condition exclusions, health-status rating, and lifetime caps, and must report how premium dollars are spent. In this draft they faced an additional threat their final law dropped: a government-run plan competing beside them in every Gateway.

The biosimilar pathway the bill creates does not permit approval of any biosimilar until 12 years after the original biologic was licensed, locking in over a decade of market exclusivity on some of the most expensive drugs. Patients and taxpayers bear the delay in price competition.
The bill gives these manufacturers a legal pathway to market cheaper copies of biologics for the first time, but the 12-year exclusivity window postpones those opportunities well into the future.

industries.industry: Chain restaurants and vending machine operators
industries.note: Chains with 20 or more locations must post calorie counts on menus and menu boards, and operators of 20 or more vending machines must post calorie signs. Compliance costs are real but modest, and consumers get calorie information at the point of sale.

Employers must pay the HHS Secretary for each worker not offered qualifying coverage or whose premiums the employer subsidizes at less than 60%, and must provide break time and a private space for nursing employees. Small employers are exempt, so the burden falls on larger firms.

The bill reauthorizes appropriations for health centers serving medically underserved populations and expands the 340B drug discount program so enrolled hospitals can also obtain inpatient drugs at discounted prices.
